title: Pulleys, gears and screws: how machines trade a small pull for a long way

summary.text: A child can lift a heavy bucket with a gentle pull, if the rope runs round the right wheels. Your child hangs a bottle from reels and a rubber band, and finds that two ropes halve the pull but double how far the hand must move. They then count the turns of a bicycle's gears, wind a paper ramp into a screw, and find where a machine's missing effort goes. They learn why pulleys, gears, screws and wedges are all the same trade, why no machine has ever given out more than it was given, and why a mathematician named Emmy Noether says that is a fact about time.
summary.art: A glass bottle of water hanging from two thread reels on a broomstick between two chairs, with a rubber band at the loose end of the string stretched to a ruler.

intro.hook: Two broom handles. One rope, wound round them several times. A strong grown-up holds the handles apart. A child pulls the end of the rope, and the handles slide together, however hard the grown-up pushes. How can a child beat a grown-up?
intro.text: The child did not become stronger. The rope did something clever. Each time it is wound round, one more length of rope pulls the handles together, so the child's pull is shared out and multiplied. In this unit you hang a bottle from two reels and count the ropes. You measure how much easier the pull gets, and how much further your hand must move. Then you follow the same idea into gears, screws and the tiny machines inside every living cell.
intro.art: A child pulling the end of a rope wound four times round two broom handles, while a grown-up at the other end tries to hold the handles apart.

outcomes: I can explain how a fixed pulley only changes the direction of a pull, and how a moving pulley shares a load between ropes. I can count the ropes that hold a load and work out the pull.
I can explain that a machine trades force for distance, so that force times distance, which scientists call work, stays the same on both sides.
I can explain where the missing effort goes in a real machine: friction turns some of it into warmth, so a real machine always needs a little more than the ideal one.
I can explain how gears and belts trade turning strength for speed, and work out how many times a small gear turns from the number of teeth.
I can explain that a screw is a ramp wound round a rod and a wedge is two ramps back to back, so the six simple machines are really two ideas, the lever and the ramp.
I can run a fair test with repeats, show the results in a table and a bar chart, and say what I thought, what I saw and why.
I can name the machines inside a scissors, a bicycle or a pressure cooker, and say why the rule that machines never give out more than they take in has never been broken.

terms.meaning: A wheel with a groove round its edge, for a rope to run over. It can change the direction of a pull, and with more than one it can make the pull smaller.
terms.example: A well has a pulley over it, so you pull down to lift the bucket up.
terms.art: A grooved wheel hung from a beam with a rope running over it and a bucket on one end.

terms.meaning: A pulley that stays hung in one place. It changes the direction of the pull, but not its size.
terms.example: A flagpole has a fixed pulley at the top, so you pull down to raise the flag.
terms.art: A flag being raised up a pole by a rope running over a wheel at the top.

terms.meaning: A pulley that hangs on the rope and rises with the load. It makes two ropes hold the load, so each rope carries half.
terms.example: A bucket hung from a wheel that sits in a loop of rope.
terms.art: A load hanging from a wheel that rests in a loop of rope, with the two rope ends going up to the beam.

terms.meaning: Several pulleys joined with one long rope. The more ropes hold the load, the smaller the pull.
terms.example: A crane lifting a heavy beam at a building site.
terms.art: Two blocks of pulleys, one above and one below, joined by a rope, lifting a heavy box.

terms.meaning: How many times a machine multiplies your push or pull. If a load of 12 kilograms needs a pull of only 3, the advantage is 4.
terms.example: Four ropes holding a load give an advantage of about 4.
terms.art: A balance with a big weight on one side and a small pull on the other, with an arrow labelled 'four times'.

terms.meaning: The push or pull on a thing, multiplied by the distance the thing moves in the direction of the push. It is a way to count how much energy was passed on.
terms.example: Lifting a bottle of 1 kilogram up by 10 centimetres is about 1 joule of work.
terms.art: A hand lifting a bottle up a ruler by 10 centimetres, with the words 'force times distance'.

terms.meaning: The scientists' unit of work and energy. One joule is the work of pushing with 1 newton for 1 metre.
terms.example: Lifting a small apple up by one metre takes about 1 joule.
terms.art: A small apple lifted by one metre beside a metre ruler.

terms.meaning: The scientists' unit of force. A 1 kilogram bottle pulls down with about 10 newtons.
terms.example: A bottle of water of 1 litre weighs about 10 newtons.
terms.art: A spring balance reading 10 newtons with a bottle of water hanging from it.

terms.meaning: How much of the work you put in comes out as useful work. The rest turns into warmth through friction.
terms.example: A well-oiled pulley may give out 9 parts in every 10 that you put in.
terms.art: An arrow of work going into a machine, with a thick useful arrow coming out and a thin wavy arrow of warmth leaving.

terms.meaning: A wheel with teeth round its edge. Its teeth fit between the teeth of another gear, so turning one turns the other.
terms.example: The gears of a bicycle are joined by a chain.
terms.art: Two toothed wheels, a big one and a small one, with their teeth meshed together.

terms.meaning: How many times one gear turns when the other turns once. You find it by dividing the number of teeth on the big gear by the number on the small one.
terms.example: A gear of 40 teeth driving a gear of 10 teeth turns it 4 times.
terms.art: A gear with 40 teeth turning once while a gear with 10 teeth turns four times, with arrows.

terms.meaning: The distance a screw moves forward in one full turn. It is the gap between one thread and the next.
terms.example: A jam jar lid rises by about 3 millimetres in each turn.
terms.art: A bolt with a ruler beside it, showing the gap between two threads.

terms.meaning: The spiral ridge wound round a screw or a bolt. It is a ramp that goes round and round.
terms.example: The ridge inside a jar lid is a thread.
terms.art: A bolt with its spiral ridge marked in a bright colour.

terms.meaning: A machine made of two or more simple machines working together.
terms.example: A pair of scissors is two levers with two wedges.
terms.art: A pair of scissors with the two levers and the two blade-wedges labelled.

terms.meaning: A loop of belt or string round two wheels, so that turning one wheel turns the other. If the wheels are different sizes, one turns faster.
terms.example: A charkha's big wheel turns a thin spindle with a belt of thread.
terms.art: A big wheel and a small wheel joined by a loop of string, with arrows showing both turning.

terms.meaning: The grip between two things that rub. It slows moving things and turns some of their movement into warmth.
terms.example: A rope rubbing on a dry wooden pulley squeals and warms up.
terms.art: A rope running over a dry wooden pulley with small wavy lines of warmth rising from the rubbing place.

explanations.concept: The fixed pulley: it only turns the pull round
explanations.definition: A fixed pulley is a wheel hung in one place with a rope over it. It changes the direction of a pull, but the pull stays the same size.
explanations.description: Think of a bucket in a well. Without a wheel, you would lean over the well and lift the bucket straight up with your arms. With a wheel over the well, you pull the rope down instead. The bucket still weighs the same, and you still pull with the same strength. Pulling down is easier because you can use your own body weight, and you can stand safely away from the edge. If the bucket needs 10 units of pull, a fixed pulley still needs 10. If you pull the rope 1 metre down, the bucket goes 1 metre up. A fixed pulley gives no advantage in strength. It gives a better direction.
examples: A flagpole has a fixed pulley at the top, so you pull down to send the flag up.
A curtain cord turns the pull along the rail round to the side.
A well with a wheel at the top lets you pull down to lift the bucket.
explanations.art: A bucket in a well with a wheel at the top, and arrows showing the rope pulled down and the bucket going up, both of the same length.
explanations.context: This card explains the simplest pulley, the one over a well, and what it does and does not do.

explanations.concept: The moving pulley and counting the ropes
explanations.definition: A moving pulley hangs on the rope and rises with the load. Count the ropes that hold the load. Each rope carries an equal share, so the pull is the load divided by the number of ropes.
explanations.description: In your test, the bottle hung from a reel that sat in a loop of string. The loop has two strands going up. Each strand holds half the bottle, so your hand only holds half. That is why the rubber band stretched about half as much. But there is a price. To lift the bottle by 10 centimetres, both strands must get 10 centimetres shorter. All that string has to come from the end you are pulling. So your hand moves 20 centimetres. With three ropes holding the load, the pull is a third and the hand moves three times as far. With four ropes, it is a quarter and four times. This is why cranes and boat sails use many pulleys and very long ropes. To count the ropes, count only the strands that touch the moving part and pull upwards on it. The strand that you hold in your hand does not count if it only passes over a fixed wheel.
examples: A load held by 2 ropes needs half the pull and twice the rope.
A load held by 4 ropes needs a quarter of the pull but 4 times the rope.
A ship's sail uses many pulleys, so a few sailors can raise a very heavy sail.
explanations.art: Three pulley set-ups side by side holding the same box. One has one rope, one has two ropes and one has four ropes, and each has a number for the pull and for the rope pulled.
explanations.context: This card explains the main result of the Count the Ropes test: how a moving pulley shares a load.

explanations.concept: Work: force times distance stays the same
explanations.definition: Work is the force on a thing multiplied by the distance it moves in the direction of the force. A machine can change the force and the distance, but the work that comes out cannot be more than the work that goes in.
explanations.description: Lifting a bottle of 1 kilogram by 10 centimetres needs a pull of about 10 newtons for 0.1 metres. Multiply them, and the work is 1 joule. With two ropes, the pull is 5 newtons and the hand moves 0.2 metres. Multiply them, and the work is again 1 joule. With four ropes, the pull is 2.5 newtons and the hand moves 0.4 metres, and the work is 1 joule once more. The numbers change but the product does not. That is the trade. A smaller force goes a longer way. We call the number of times a machine multiplies your force its mechanical advantage. A machine with an advantage of 2 needs half the force and twice the distance. No set-up of ropes, levers or ramps has ever given out more work than was put in.
examples: 1 kilogram lifted 10 centimetres: 10 newtons times 0.1 metres is 1 joule.
The same lift with 2 ropes: 5 newtons times 0.2 metres is still 1 joule.
A ramp 4 times as long as the height needs a quarter of the push.
explanations.art: Three boxes showing 10 newtons times 0.1 metres, 5 newtons times 0.2 metres and 2.5 newtons times 0.4 metres, all equal to 1 joule.
explanations.context: This card explains the number that stays the same however you arrange the ropes: force times distance.

explanations.concept: Where the missing effort goes: friction and efficiency
explanations.definition: In a real machine, some of the work you put in turns into warmth through friction. Efficiency is the part of the work that comes out as useful work.
explanations.description: In your test, two ropes should have halved the pull. But the rubber band probably stretched a little more than half. The reel rubbed on its pencil and the string rubbed on the reel. That rubbing turned some of your effort into warmth, which spread into the air. The work did not disappear. It went somewhere you did not want it. A pulley with an efficiency of 90 percent gives out 90 parts of useful work for every 100 you put in. The other 10 parts become warmth. Oil on an axle, a smooth wheel and a ball bearing all cut the rubbing. Adding more machines adds more rubbing, and their losses multiply. Two machines that are each 90 percent efficient together give 0.9 times 0.9, which is 81 percent. That is why more machines are not always better.
examples: A dry wooden pulley squeals and warms up, so it wastes more than an oiled one.
A bicycle chain with oil on it wastes less of the rider's effort.
Two machines of 90 percent each give 81 percent together.
explanations.art: A pulley with two thin arrows of work going in and a thick arrow coming out, and small wavy lines of warmth leaving from the axle and the rope.
explanations.context: This card explains why your real results were a little worse than the ideal numbers.

explanations.concept: Gears: trading turning strength for speed
explanations.definition: A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears mesh, the smaller one turns more times than the bigger one. The ratio is the number of teeth on the big gear divided by the number on the small one.
explanations.description: A bicycle has a big gear at the pedals and a small gear at the back wheel. The big gear has about 44 teeth and the small one has about 18. For every turn of the pedals, the chain moves 44 teeth. That is enough to turn the small gear 44 divided by 18, which is about 2.4 times. So one turn of your feet turns the wheel 2.4 times, and the bicycle goes fast. But there is a price. The wheel turns with less strength than your feet put in. If you want strength, for example to climb a hill, you choose a bigger gear at the back. Then the wheel turns fewer times for each pedal turn, but it turns with more strength. This is the same trade as the ropes. Strength and speed can be swapped, but you cannot get both. A belt drive, like the string on a charkha, does the same, with two wheels and a belt instead of teeth.
examples: A gear of 40 teeth turning a gear of 10 teeth makes the small one spin 4 times for each turn.
A cycle's low gear for a hill has a big gear at the back and turns the wheel fewer times.
A charkha's big wheel turns a thin spindle many times, so the thread twists quickly.
explanations.art: A bicycle chain going from a big gear at the pedals to a small gear at the back wheel, with the teeth counts and the turns written beside them.
explanations.context: This card explains what you find in the bicycle gear test: why the wheel turns more than once for each pedal turn.

explanations.concept: The screw: a ramp wound round a rod
explanations.definition: A screw is a ramp wound round and round a rod. The pitch is how far it moves forward in one full turn.
explanations.description: Imagine a ramp of 30 centimetres that climbs 1 centimetre. It is a very gentle slope, so a small push moves a load up it. Now wind that ramp round a pencil. It becomes a spiral, the thread of a screw. One turn of the screw takes you along one gap of the thread, which is the pitch. If the pitch is 2 millimetres, then 10 turns move the screw 20 millimetres. Each turn is a long, gentle walk up the ramp, so a small twist makes a strong push forward. That is why a screw can hold two pieces of wood together so tightly, and why a jar lid squeezes the jar shut. A screw jack lifts a car this way. The Archimedes screw, a spiral inside a tube, lifts water. Farmers on the Nile used it, and it was used in many places later.
examples: A jam jar lid goes down about 3 millimetres each full turn.
A screw jack lifts a car with turns of a handle.
An Archimedes screw lifts water up a tube when its spiral is turned.
explanations.art: A paper triangle wound round a pencil so its sloping edge becomes a spiral, beside a bolt with the same spiral and a ruler measuring the gap between two threads.
explanations.context: This card explains how the paper ramp you wind in the Paper Screw activity becomes a screw.

explanations.concept: The wedge: two ramps that push things apart
explanations.definition: A wedge is two ramps back to back, with a thin edge at the front. Pushing it in pushes the material aside, with a force bigger than the push, over a smaller distance.
explanations.description: When you push a wedge into a log, the thin edge goes in only a short way, while the two sloping sides push the wood apart. The thinner the wedge, the longer and gentler its sloping sides, and the more it multiplies your push. A knife is a wedge. When it is sharpened, it gets thinner, so it cuts with less push. A blunt knife needs more push because it is a thick wedge. Your front teeth are wedges, for biting through an apple. A nail, a needle and the bow of a boat are wedges as well. A wedge works best along a line where the material wants to split. Wood splits along the grain far more easily than across it, and an axe or a knife slips in along the weak line.
examples: A knife gets easier to use when it is sharpened, because the wedge is thinner.
A door stop is a wedge that holds a door by jamming under it.
A chisel splits wood along the grain much more easily than across it.
explanations.art: A thin wedge and a thick wedge pushed into two blocks of wood, with arrows showing the sideways push, which is bigger for the thin wedge.
explanations.context: This card explains the wedge as two ramps, the second of the two machines that are really ramps.

explanations.definition: The lever, the wheel and axle and the pulley are all kinds of lever. The ramp, the wedge and the screw are all kinds of ramp. Both ideas follow one rule: force times distance stays the same.
explanations.description: In Class 3 you met six simple machines. Look closely and they share their insides. A pulley is a lever with equal arms bent round into a wheel, and a moving pulley is a lever with arms in a ratio of 2 to 1. A wheel and axle is a lever that goes round and round, with the handle at the long end. A wedge is two ramps back to back, and a screw is a ramp wound round a rod. So six names, two ideas. A lever swaps force and distance by moving a fulcrum. A ramp swaps force and distance by changing the slope. Whichever you pick, the trade is the same. A smaller force goes a longer way. People sorted these machines into six kinds because they look different, and that sorting helps us remember them. But the sorting is ours. Nature has only one rule underneath.
examples: A moving pulley is a lever in which the load hangs from the middle and the effort is at the end.
A screw is a ramp wound round a rod.
A wheel and axle, such as a well winch, is a lever that goes round.
explanations.art: Six small machines in two columns. A lever, a pulley and a wheel and axle on the left, and a ramp, a wedge and a screw on the right, with a line joining each to its idea.
explanations.context: This card shows that the six machines from Class 3 are really only two ideas.

explanations.concept: Compound machines: machines made from machines
explanations.definition: A compound machine is made of two or more simple machines. Its total advantage is found by multiplying the advantages of its parts, but each part also adds friction.
explanations.description: A pair of scissors is two levers, joined at a screw or rivet, with a wedge on the end of each lever. A bicycle holds levers (the pedals and the brakes), wheels and axles, gears and screws. A wheelbarrow is a lever with a wheel at the end. A pressure cooker lid is a screw-like lock. A hand pump has a lever handle and a piston. In every one, ask the same two questions. What does each part trade, force for distance or the other way round? And where does the friction come from? If a lever with an advantage of 3 pushes a wedge with an advantage of 4, together they multiply to 12. But the friction in both parts takes a share of the work.
examples: Scissors: two levers and two wedges.
A bicycle: levers, wheels and axles, gears and screws.
A wheelbarrow: a lever with a wheel at the end.
explanations.art: A bicycle with its levers, gears, wheels and axle, and screws labelled in different colours.
explanations.context: This card shows how everyday tools are put together from the simple machines in this unit.

explanations.concept: Machines smaller than a speck: motors inside living cells
explanations.definition: Living cells contain tiny machines made of protein. One of them is a rotary motor that turns like a wheel on an axle.
explanations.description: A bacterium swims by spinning a long thread called a flagellum. In 1973, Howard Berg and Robert Anderson suggested that it turns round like a propeller on a motor. In 1974, Michael Silverman and Melvin Simon proved it. They stuck the thread to a glass slide, and the whole cell spun round instead. The motor can turn hundreds of times a second. Another tiny motor, called ATP synthase, sits in the cells of plants, animals and bacteria. It turns like a wheel on an axle and makes the fuel molecule ATP. In 1997 Hiroyuki Noji and his team in Japan fixed one to glass, put a tiny glowing rod on it, and watched it turn under a microscope. The rule of this unit still holds at this size. Each motor takes energy in and gives some out, and a little escapes as warmth.
examples: The bacterium's flagellar motor spins a thread to swim.
ATP synthase turns like a wheel and makes the fuel ATP in your cells, and in every plant.
Muscle proteins in your arm work like tiny levers.
explanations.art: A bacterium with a long thread, and a zoomed-in drawing of the ring-shaped motor at the base where the thread joins the cell.
explanations.context: This card takes the wheel and axle down to the smallest size, inside a single cell.

explanations.concept: Why machines can never give out more: energy and time
explanations.definition: Energy is never made from nothing or destroyed, only moved or changed. In 1918 Emmy Noether showed that this follows from the laws of nature being the same on every day.
explanations.description: Everything in this unit has the same ending. However you arrange the ropes, the work that comes out is never more than the work that went in. For thousands of years inventors tried to build machines that gave out extra, and none worked. Energy is the thing that is passed on. It can change from a pull to height, or to warmth, but the total stays. In 1918, the German mathematician Emmy Noether showed something deeper. If the laws of nature do not change from one day to the next, then energy cannot be made or lost. The rule is not about ropes. It is about time. Noether did this at a university where, for years, she was not allowed to be a paid teacher, and her lectures were announced under a male professor's name. Physicists say the rule gets tricky when the whole universe is stretching, and this is still being discussed.
examples: A pulley, a lever and a ramp all show the same total work in and out.
A swing swings lower each time as friction turns its energy into warmth, but the total stays the same.
A battery, a bulb and the warm wire together keep the same total energy.
explanations.art: A pulley, a lever and a ramp each with 'work in' and 'work out' arrows of equal size, and Emmy Noether's portrait in a corner.
explanations.context: This card explains why no machine has ever beaten the trade, and what a mathematician found out about it.

explanations.concept: Who made the first wheels, pulleys and gears?
explanations.definition: Nobody knows who first made these machines. We have only the oldest things that survived, and some of them are very surprising.
explanations.description: The oldest wheel with an axle that we know of was found in a marsh near Ljubljana in Slovenia in 2002. Tree rings in the wood of the wheel show that it is about 5,000 years old. In the Indus cities, such as Harappa, people made little carts with wheels from clay and bronze about 4,500 years ago. The oldest pulleys that we know of come from Mesopotamia and Egypt, perhaps 3,500 years ago or more, but only a few survive, because rope and wood rot. The most amazing old machine is the Antikythera mechanism, found in 1901 in a shipwreck off a Greek island. It is more than 2,000 years old and has more than 30 bronze gears. It showed where the Sun and Moon would be and could predict eclipses. After that, no machine so complex is known for over a thousand years. Historians still argue about who made it and where.
examples: A wheel with an axle from a marsh in Slovenia, about 5,000 years old.
Little wheeled carts from Harappan towns, about 4,500 years old.
The Antikythera mechanism, a Greek gear machine more than 2,000 years old.
explanations.art: The Antikythera mechanism as a drawing: a bronze box with many gears of different sizes and a dial on the front.
explanations.context: This card tells what we know, and do not know, about when people first built these machines.

agreed.text: A fixed pulley changes the direction of a pull, and a moving pulley divides the pull between the ropes that hold the load.
agreed.evidence: Spring balances and rubber bands show the pull in each rope, and it halves each time the number of supporting ropes doubles.

agreed.text: A simple machine can make a force smaller, but only by making its distance longer. The work in and the work out are equal in an ideal machine.
agreed.evidence: Careful measurements of levers, ramps, pulleys and gears have always shown force times distance staying equal.

agreed.text: In real machines, friction turns some of the work into warmth, so the work out is always a little less than the work in.
agreed.evidence: Pulleys, axles and gears feel warm after use, and oiling them reduces the loss.

agreed.text: A gear that turns more slowly gives more turning strength, and a gear that turns faster gives less.
agreed.evidence: Cyclists use low gears for hills and high gears on flat roads, and the tooth counts predict the turns exactly.

agreed.text: A screw is a ramp wound round a rod, and a wedge is two ramps back to back.
agreed.evidence: If you unwrap the thread of a screw, it makes a ramp of a fixed slope.

agreed.text: Living cells contain tiny rotary motors that turn like wheels on axles.
agreed.evidence: Silverman and Simon in 1974 and Noji and others in 1997 watched them turn under microscopes.

challenging.claim: A pulley makes the load lighter.
challenging.for: It feels easier to pull down than to lift.
challenging.against: A single pulley changes only the direction of the pull. The pull is the same as the weight of the load. Only more ropes holding the load make the pull smaller.

challenging.claim: With enough clever wheels, a machine can give out more work than you put in.
challenging.who: Inventors of 'perpetual motion' machines, for hundreds of years.
challenging.for: Levers and pulleys seem to multiply your strength.
challenging.against: They multiply force but shorten the distance, so the work is the same. Every attempt to beat the trade has failed.

challenging.claim: The more machines you add, the easier the job becomes.
challenging.for: Each machine can multiply the force.
challenging.against: Each machine also adds friction and wastes a share of the work. Two machines of 90 percent efficiency give only 81 percent.

challenging.claim: A bigger gear always makes things go faster.
challenging.for: A big gear at the pedals turns a small gear many times.
challenging.against: It depends on which gear drives which. A big gear driving a small one is faster. A small gear driving a big one is slower, but stronger.

challenging.claim: Archimedes could have moved the Earth with a lever if he had a long enough one and a place to stand.
challenging.who: Archimedes' saying, written down by later writers such as Pappus of Alexandria.
challenging.for: The law of the lever has no upper limit on the size of the load.
challenging.against: The lever would have to be about as wide as our whole galaxy, and he would have to push his end for that whole length to lift the Earth by one centimetre. Nobody can build a fixed place to stand.

big_questions.q: A ramp has no moving parts. Is a ramp really a machine, and is a hill a machine too?
big_questions.hint: Think about what makes something a machine: its parts, or what it does to a push.

big_questions.q: The six simple machines are two ideas. Who decided how to count them, nature or people?
big_questions.hint: Think about what we notice first, and what the rule underneath says.

big_questions.q: No machine has ever given out more than it took in. Is that a fact about machines, or about the universe?
big_questions.hint: Think about Emmy Noether's idea about the laws being the same on every day.

big_questions.q: A bicycle is slow up a hill in a high gear and fast on the flat in a low one. Why can't we have both at once?
big_questions.hint: Think about the rope test, where you could swap pull for distance but not get both.

big_questions.q: A bacterium has a tiny wheel on an axle, but no wheel ever evolved in the legs of a large animal. Why might that be?
big_questions.hint: Think about blood, nerves and the way a wheel needs a clear path all around it.

big_questions.q: A machine takes the same work from a strong person and a weak person. Is it fair that machines are mostly built for the people who already have power?
big_questions.hint: Think about who owns a crane, a well pump or a mill, and who works it.

big_questions.q: Some people ask whether an ant, a plant's root or a cell could be called a machine. What is a living body, if it is more than a machine?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tiny motors in your cells, and whether a machine can decide anything.

big_questions.q: When a bullock pulls a rope, the bullock is the engine and the pulley is the machine. Who is doing the work?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the energy came from: the grass, and before the grass, the Sun.

story.title: Twice the Rope
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Leather-bucket well lifts pulled by bullocks are real, and are called a mote in Karnataka and a charsa in the North. The names and what happened are imagined.
text: On the farm near Gadag where Nagaveni lived, the well was older than anyone in the family. Her grandmother, Ajji, still watered the jowar every morning with the old well lift.

It was a leather bag as big as a barrel, hanging from a thick rope. The rope ran over a wooden wheel at the edge of the well and then along the ground to two bullocks, Bangara and Rama. When the bullocks walked down the sloping path, the rope pulled, and the bag came up full of water. At the top, it tipped into the channel. Then the bullocks walked back, and the bag went down again.

That summer the rain did not come. The water sank lower. Each morning, the bag had to climb a longer way, and each morning, it came up heavier with mud. On the fifth day, Bangara stopped halfway down the path. He leaned into the yoke and breathed hard. The rope stayed tight and the bag stayed in the dark of the well.
'They are tired,' said Ajji. 'They are too old for this well now.'
Their neighbour, Basavanna, was leaning on the wall. 'Buy a third bullock,' he said. 'Or wait for the rain. There is no other way.'

Nagaveni had come back from school that week with a lesson in her head. In class, her teacher had hung a bottle of water from two thread reels and a string. A rubber band at the end of the string showed how hard each pull was. With the right reels, the band stretched only half as far.
'Ajji,' she said, 'what if the bag hung from a second wheel?'
Basavanna laughed. 'A wheel cannot make water lighter, child.'

'No,' said Nagaveni. 'The water weighs the same. But look.' She took a stick and drew in the dust. 'Now there is one rope going up to the wheel at the top. If the bag hangs on a wheel of its own, in the loop of the rope, there are two ropes holding the bag. Each rope holds half. Bangara will feel half.'
'And where does the other half go?' asked Basavanna.
'Nowhere,' she said. 'It is paid in walking. To raise the bag by one step, both ropes must get one step shorter. So the bullocks must walk two steps. The bag will come up half as fast.'
Basavanna rubbed his chin. 'Then it is the same work. They walk twice as far.'

'The same work,' Nagaveni agreed. 'But Bangara can pull a certain weight, and he stops at a bit more than that. He is not too tired to walk. He is too weak for this pull. If the pull is half, he can walk all day.'
Ajji looked at the well, and then at the path. The path ran down the slope, past the cowshed and as far as the stone wall of the field. It was twelve metres long. The water was now eight metres down.
'Twice eight is sixteen,' said Nagaveni, who had counted. 'The path is only twelve metres, Ajji. We need four more.'

Everyone looked at Basavanna, because the wall beyond was his. He sighed. Then he walked to the wall and lifted down the top three stones. 'Let them turn along my field edge,' he said. 'Just this summer.'

They tied the end of the rope to the wooden frame. Nagaveni hung the bag from a spare wooden wheel from the carpenter, and ran the rope round it and back up. Then she tied her school rubber band into the rope, to see how hard the pull was. With one rope, the band had stretched long and thin. Now it stretched only a little more than half as far.
'A little more than half,' she said. 'The wheels are dry. They are rubbing.'
Ajji went to the kitchen and came back with a little coconut oil on a rag. She rubbed it into the axle of both wheels. The squeal went away, and the band shortened a little more.

Bangara and Rama leaned into the yoke. The bag rose slowly out of the dark with the water swinging in it. The bullocks walked down the path, and past the cowshed, and along the edge of Basavanna's field, a long, slow walk. Neither of them stopped.
When the bag tipped into the channel and the water ran down between the rows of jowar, Basavanna took off his cap.
'Twice the rope,' he said. 'Half the pull.'
'And twice the time,' said Nagaveni. 'There is always a price.'
Ajji watched the water run. 'It is a fair price,' she said. 'The bullocks pay it in walking, and they have legs for that.'
story.epiphany: Count the ropes that hold the load. Each rope carries an equal share. The pull is the load divided by the number of ropes, and the walk is that many times longer.
ask: Why did the bullocks have to walk twice as far when the bag hung from two ropes?
What would happen to the pull and to the walk if the bag hung from four ropes?
Why did the oil on the wheels make the pull a little smaller?

roots.context: We have counted ropes, turned gears and found that every machine trades a smaller pull for a longer way. Now we ask why that trade never changes, and what it tells us.

deep_truth.truth: With every set of reels, the hand moved exactly as much further as the pull got smaller. In 1918 Emmy Noether showed why. If the laws of nature work the same on every day, energy cannot be made from nothing. So no machine can cheat, because cheating would need nature to change its rules from day to day.
deep_truth.habit: We treat 'you cannot get something for nothing' as a fact about ropes and levers, a limit of the tools that we make. It is a wider rule, tied to how time works.
deep_truth.evidence: In the rope test, a fixed reel only turned the pull round, and a moving reel halved the pull and doubled the distance. Force times distance came out about the same each time, a little worse because of friction.

three.who_am_i: You can lift more than your strength alone if you share the load between ropes. What you can do depends on how you arrange things.
three.what_is_life: Inside every cell of your body, tiny motors turn like wheels on axles, and they follow the same trade as a pulley.
three.what_is_this_world: No machine anywhere, from a crane to a cell, has beaten the trade of force for distance. That is because the world's laws stay the same on every day.

roots.thread: Six machines turned out to be two ideas, and the two ideas turned out to be one trade. Behind the trade is a single rule about energy, which Emmy Noether linked to the way time behaves. Rope, wood, steel and protein all follow it. The many tools and cells are different shapes of the same rule. A rope pulled by a girl, a bullock or a motor passes on energy it received from somewhere, and that, in the end, came from the Sun.

teachings.teaching: The way of heaven is like bending a bow. What is high is brought down, and what is low is raised. It takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little.
teachings.link: A lever or pulley takes from the distance and gives to the force, so the two stay in balance.

teachings.teaching: People do not see how something that pulls against itself can still hold together, like the tension of a bow and a lyre.
teachings.link: A rope that is pulled at both ends holds a load. The pull in the rope and the weight of the load hold each other in balance.

teachings.teaching: Cook Ding cut up an ox for 19 years with one knife that never went blunt. He did not cut through the bones, but slid his thin blade through the gaps between them.
teachings.link: A wedge works best along a line where a material already wants to split, so the thinnest edge does the most with the least push.

science.text: Emmy Noether's theorem of 1918: every steady symmetry of nature's laws has a conserved quantity. Laws that are the same on every day mean that energy is conserved.
In the whole expanding universe, energy is harder to define, and physicists still argue about whether it is conserved overall.

other_view.who: Henri Poincare, a French mathematician, in 1902
other_view.view: Poincare argued that the rule of energy may partly be our choice of how to keep books. When energy seemed to go missing in some atoms in the 1920s, Wolfgang Pauli suggested in 1930 a new invisible particle rather than give up the rule. The neutrino was found in 1956. Poincare would say we chose to keep the rule, and nature agreed. Others say nature chose the rule first.

practice.title: The long way round
practice.say: Stand at one end of a room. Walk to the far end in a wide zig-zag, slowly, taking about 20 steps. Breathe out on each step. Notice that the long way asks very little of each step. Then walk straight across quickly, and notice the difference.
practice.kid: Walk across the room in a slow zig-zag. Breathe out on each step. Notice how little each step asks. Then walk straight across fast.

ask: If nature has only one trade, why do we count six machines?
Is the rule that machines never give more than they take a discovery about nature, or a choice that we made about how to keep count?
If the laws of nature changed from day to day, what would a machine do?
