games.title: Rope Counter: how big is the pull, and how far do I walk?
games.context: This is a card game about the trade you found with the reels. Each card describes a load and a machine. You work out the pull or the distance, then turn the card over to check.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile, with a pencil and a strip of paper for each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while each other player writes a number on a scrap of paper.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone writes their answer.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the answer, and players holding up their scraps of paper to compare.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Check the answers together.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a load and a machine on the front, and the pull and the distance on the back

items.f: A sack of 12 kilograms hangs from one rope over one fixed pulley. You lift it 2 metres. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 12 kilograms. Hand: 2 metres. A fixed pulley only turns the pull round.

items.f: A sack of 12 kilograms hangs from a moving pulley, with 2 ropes holding it. You lift it 2 metres. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 6 kilograms. Hand: 4 metres. 12 divided by 2 is 6, and 2 times 2 is 4.

items.f: A box of 20 kilograms is held by 4 ropes. You lift it 1 metre. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 5 kilograms. Hand: 4 metres. 20 divided by 4 is 5.

items.f: A water can of 15 kilograms is held by 3 ropes. You lift it 2 metres. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 5 kilograms. Hand: 6 metres. 15 divided by 3 is 5, and 2 times 3 is 6.

items.f: A crate of 25 kilograms is held by 5 ropes. You lift it 1 metre. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 5 kilograms. Hand: 5 metres.

items.f: A bucket of 8 kilograms is held by 2 ropes. You lift it 3 metres. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 4 kilograms. Hand: 6 metres.

items.f: A load of 30 kilograms hangs from one moving pulley, with 2 ropes holding it. The rope then goes over a fixed pulley at the top, so you pull down. You lift the load 1 metre. How heavy is the pull?
items.b: Pull: 15 kilograms. Hand: 2 metres. The fixed pulley only turns the pull round. It adds no rope under the load.

items.f: A block and tackle has 6 ropes holding a load of 30 kilograms. You lift it 2 metres. How heavy is the pull, and how far does your hand move?
items.b: Pull: 5 kilograms. Hand: 12 metres.

items.f: You pull with 4 kilograms to raise a box of 16 kilograms. How many ropes hold the box?
items.b: 4 ropes. 16 divided by 4 is 4.

items.f: A building-site crane has a block and tackle with 5 ropes holding a load of 100 kilograms. What is the smallest pull the rope could have, if there is no friction?
items.b: 20 kilograms. 100 divided by 5 is 20. With friction, the real pull is a bit more.

items.f: A 4-rope tackle lifts 40 kilograms. With no friction the pull would be 10 kilograms. In real life you pull with 13 kilograms. About what share of your effort is useful? Say 'about 8 in every 10' or 'about 6 in every 10'.
items.b: About 8 in every 10. Useful share is 10 divided by 13, which is about 0.77. The rest turned into warmth.

items.f: A drum of 20 kilograms is rolled up a ramp 4 metres long to a platform 1 metre high. Roughly what push does it need, and how far do you push? Ignore friction.
items.b: Push: about 5 kilograms. Distance: 4 metres. The ramp is 4 times as long as the height.

items.f: The same drum of 20 kilograms is rolled up a ramp that is 2 metres long, to the same 1 metre high platform. Roughly what push does it need? Ignore friction.
items.b: Push: about 10 kilograms. The ramp is 2 times as long as the height, so the push is half of 20.

items.f: A crowbar is a lever. A load of 40 kilograms is 10 centimetres from the fulcrum. You push 40 centimetres from the fulcrum. What push do you need?
items.b: 10 kilograms. 40 times 10 is 400, and 400 divided by 40 is 10. Your end moves 4 times as far.

items.f: A lever has a load of 30 kilograms at 20 centimetres from the fulcrum. You push 60 centimetres from it. What push do you need, and how many times as far does your end move?
items.b: Push: 10 kilograms. Your end moves 3 times as far as the load.

items.f: A gear with 36 teeth turns a gear with 12 teeth. For one turn of the big gear, how many turns does the small gear make?
items.b: 3 turns. 36 divided by 12 is 3.

items.f: A gear with 40 teeth turns a gear with 10 teeth. For one turn of the big gear, how many turns does the small gear make?
items.b: 4 turns. 40 divided by 10 is 4.

items.f: A small gear with 12 teeth turns a big gear with 36 teeth. For one turn of the small gear, how much does the big gear turn?
items.b: One third of a turn. It is slower, but it turns with more strength.

items.f: A bicycle has 48 teeth at the pedals and 16 teeth at the back wheel. For one turn of the pedals, how many turns does the back wheel make?
items.b: 3 turns. 48 divided by 16 is 3.

items.f: The same bicycle changes to a back gear with 24 teeth for climbing a hill. For one turn of the pedals, how many turns does the back wheel make now? Is it faster or slower?
items.b: 2 turns. 48 divided by 24 is 2. It is slower, but the wheel turns with more strength.

items.f: A screw has a pitch of 2 millimetres. How far does it move in 10 full turns?
items.b: 20 millimetres. 10 times 2 is 20.

items.f: A jar lid must rise 6 millimetres to come off. The pitch of its thread is 3 millimetres. How many full turns does it need?
items.b: 2 turns. 6 divided by 3 is 2.

items.f: You must split a log with a wedge. Which needs less push, a thin wedge or a thick wedge? Why?
items.b: A thin wedge. Its sloping sides are a longer, gentler ramp, so it multiplies your push more.

items.f: A belt joins a big wheel, 30 centimetres across, to a small wheel, 10 centimetres across. For one turn of the big wheel, how many turns does the small wheel make?
items.b: 3 turns. 30 divided by 10 is 3.

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, but does not show the back.
Every other player writes down their answer on a scrap of paper. Some cards ask for two numbers, and some ask for one.
The reader turns the card and reads the back. Each correct number scores one point.
A player who also says how many ropes hold the load, or which machine it is, scores one more point.
With two players, the parent and the child swap the reader's job after every card.
To play alone, read a card, write your answer, turn the card over and mark yourself. Try to beat your own score next time.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile. Give each player a scrap of paper and a pencil.
flow.say: These cards show a load and a machine. We work out the pull and the distance. Then we turn the card over to check.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Get paper and a pencil.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rope Counter. You set up the cards.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the front. Everyone writes an answer. Now turn the card over. Who got the pull? Who got the distance?
flow.kid: Read a card. Write your answer. Turn the card to check.

ask.q: What do you notice about the pull and the distance as you add ropes?
good: The pull gets smaller and the distance gets bigger.
When one doubles, the other halves.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn the pattern.

flow.do: Play the next ten cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Count only the ropes that hold the load. A fixed pulley at the top does not add a rope under the load.
flow.kid: Play on. Count the ropes that hold the load.

ask.q: Which card was the trickiest, and why?
good: The one with a fixed pulley on top.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about what trades with what. Is it force and distance, or turns and strength?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card taught them the most, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card taught you the most? Why?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card taught you most? Why?
flow.think: Is there any card where you could get a smaller pull and a shorter distance at the same time?
flow.context: This is the last step of Rope Counter. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Count the Ropes: how much easier does a pulley make a lift, and what does it cost?
experiments.question: A bottle of water hangs from a rubber band. Does the band stretch less if the string goes over one fixed reel, or if a moving reel shares the load between two strings? And how far must the string move?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which of the three ways will the rubber band stretch least? Will the string move further in any of them? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same bottle, the same rubber band and the same 10 centimetre lift are used every time. Only the way the string runs changes. The straight lift is the control. Each way is done twice, so one odd try does not mislead you.
results_table: Distance the knot moved for a 10 centimetre lift, in centimetres

materials.item: a plastic bottle of 1 litre, full of water, with a string loop tied round its neck
2 empty thread reels, or 2 round plastic bangles
about 3 metres of strong thin string, such as nylon cord
a rubber band that stretches 6 to 12 centimetres when the full bottle hangs from it
a broom handle, to rest across two chair backs, or a bar of a window grill
a ruler or tape measure, and a stack of books about 10 centimetres tall
tape, a pen, the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up must check that the beam is tied down and holds the bottle. Keep feet away from under the bottle in case it falls.
experiments.record: For each set-up, write the stretch of the band on both tries, and how far the knot moved for a 10 centimetre lift. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each set-up, using the bigger of the two stretches.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you lift a bottle three ways and use a rubber band to feel the pull. You find out what a fixed reel and a moving reel really do.

setup.art: A thread reel with a short string loop through its hole, hanging from a broom handle laid across two chair backs.
setup.caption: 1. Make a reel hang from a string loop. Hang it from the beam.

setup.art: A bottle of water hanging by a string from a rubber band held in a hand, with a ruler beside the band.
setup.caption: 2. Test A: hang the bottle straight from the band and measure the stretch.

setup.art: A string from the bottle going up over the hanging reel and down to a rubber band in a hand, with a stack of books beside the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Test B: run the string over one fixed reel and pull down.

setup.art: A bottle hanging from a second reel in a loop of string, with one end of the string tied to the beam and the other going over the fixed reel to a band.
setup.caption: 4. Test C: hang the bottle from a moving reel, with two strings holding it.

setup.art: Three bars of different heights, one for each way of lifting, with a number on each bar.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each way, using the bigger stretch.

flow.do: Show your child the bottle, the reels, the band and the string. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will lift this bottle three ways. First straight up. Then over one reel. Then with a moving reel as well. In which way will the band stretch least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three ways to lift a bottle. Which way stretches the band least? Why?

ask.q: Do you think the string will move further in any of the three ways?
good: Yes, in the one with more string.
No, the bottle lifts the same height.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say more reels always make it easier. Write down exactly what they say and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Ropes. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Thread string through the hole of each reel and knot it into a loop. Tie a loop round the bottle's neck. Tie the broom handle across two chair backs. Check it holds the bottle.
flow.say: Each reel hangs from its own string loop and can spin on it. Hang one reel from the beam. This is our fixed reel. Now measure the band with nothing on it, and write that length down.
flow.kid: Make a string loop through each reel. Hang one from the beam. Measure the band with nothing on it.
flow.parent: A grown-up should do the beam and check it. The thread reels from a tailor are free. If a reel will not spin easily, widen the loop. A bangle works too, but it rubs more, so your pull will be bigger. That is part of the lesson.

check.q: Why do you measure the band with nothing hanging on it first?
options: So you can work out how much it stretched
check.why: The stretch is the new length minus the starting length. Without the starting length, you could not say how much the band stretched.

flow.context: In this step, you build the pulleys and the beam, and measure the band at rest.

flow.do: Test A. Tie the bottle's string to the band. Hold the band's top end. Lift the bottle until its base is level with the top of the 10 centimetre stack of books. Hold still and read the band. Do it twice.
flow.say: Lift slowly, then hold still, and read the band's length. The stretch is the length now minus the length with nothing on it. Write it down. Do it twice.
flow.kid: Hang the bottle from the band. Lift it 10 centimetres. Hold still. Read the band.

ask.q: Why do we hold still before we read the band?
good: Because a moving band is hard to read.
So we get the same answer each time.

flow.parent: A good band stretches 6 to 12 centimetres. If it stretches less than 4, use a thinner band. If it nearly snaps, use two bands side by side. For this set-up, the knot moves 10 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step, you do the straight lift. It is the control.

flow.do: Test B. Tie one end of the string to the bottle's loop. Run it up over the fixed reel and down to the band. Hold the band's other end and pull down until the bottle is 10 centimetres up. Hold still and read the band. Do it twice.
flow.say: Now the string goes over the reel. You pull down. Lift the bottle until it reaches the same height. Hold still. What does the band say? How far did the knot move?
flow.kid: String over the reel. Pull down. Lift the bottle 10 centimetres. Read the band.

check.q: In Test B the band stretches about the same as in Test A. What did the fixed reel do?
options: It changed the direction of the pull
check.why: The fixed reel turned the pull round, so you pull down instead of up. The band stretched about the same, so the pull did not get smaller. Picking 'lighter' means the reel was thought to change the bottle, but only the direction changed.

flow.parent: The stretch is usually the same, or a little bigger, because of rubbing. The knot moves 10 centimetres, down. Measure its height at the start and at the end if you want to be sure.
flow.context: In this step, you pull the bottle up over one fixed reel.

flow.do: Test C. Tie one end of the string to the beam. Run it down under the second reel, which the bottle hangs from. Then take it up over the fixed reel and down to the band. Pull down until the bottle is 10 centimetres up. Hold still, read the band and measure the knot's height at the start and the end. Do it twice.
flow.say: Now the bottle hangs from a moving reel. Count the strings that touch the moving reel. How many hold the bottle? Pull down and lift it 10 centimetres. What does the band say now? How far did the knot go?
flow.kid: Hang the bottle from the moving reel. Count the strings holding it. Pull. Read the band.

ask.q: How many strings hold up the bottle in this set-up?
good: Two, because the string goes under the reel and back up.
The one over the top does not hold it, it only turns the pull.

check.q: In Test C the band stretches about half as much as in Test A, and the knot moves about twice as far. What does this show?
options: Two strings share the load, so each carries half, but all the string must be pulled twice as far
The moving reel made the bottle weigh half as much
check.why: Each string carries half the load, so the pull is about half. To raise the bottle 10 centimetres, both strings must get 10 centimetres shorter, so the knot moves 20 centimetres. Picking 'weigh half' means the load was thought to change, but only the share each string carries changed.

flow.parent: The stretch is usually a little more than half of Test A, because of rubbing. The knot should move about 20 centimetres. If the stretch is exactly the same as A, check that the string runs under the moving reel. Count the strings that touch it.
flow.context: In this step, you hang the bottle from a moving reel and find out what two strings do.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with one bar for each way, using the bigger of the two stretches. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see in the table? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each way. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: The stretch got smaller and the knot moved further. What stayed the same?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the fixed reel only changed direction, and that the moving reel halved the pull but doubled the distance. After they have said what they saw, explain it. A bottle of 1 kilogram needs about 10 newtons. Lifting it 0.1 metres is 1 joule of work. With two strings, the pull is about 5 newtons and the knot moves 0.2 metres, which is again 1 joule. The extra stretch in your results is friction.
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Ropes. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Bicycle Gears: how many times does the wheel turn for one turn of the pedals?
experiments.question: When you turn the pedal of a bicycle once, how many times does the back wheel turn, and does the number of teeth on the gears tell you?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many times will the back wheel turn for one turn of the pedals? Will it be more than once or less? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same bicycle, the same gear and the same tape mark are used every time. You turn the pedals exactly one full turn, slowly, three times. Then you compare the counted turns with the number worked out from the teeth.
results_table: Wheel turns counted for one pedal turn
Wheel turns worked out from the teeth

materials.item: a bicycle with a chain, such as a single-speed cycle
a small piece of coloured tape or chalk to mark the back tyre
a second piece of tape to mark one tooth of the pedal gear
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up must turn the bicycle upside down onto its seat and handlebars, or lift the back wheel on a stand. Keep fingers away from the chain and the teeth, because they can pinch.
experiments.record: Write the number of teeth on each gear, the number of wheel turns you counted for each pedal turn, and the number you worked out by dividing the teeth.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you count the teeth on a bicycle's gears and the turns of its wheel, and find the gear ratio.

setup.art: A bicycle upside down on its seat and handlebars, with a bright tape mark on the back tyre and another on one tooth of the pedal gear.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up turns the bicycle upside down. Stick tape on the tyre and on one tooth.

setup.art: A child counting the teeth of the big pedal gear with a finger, starting from the taped tooth.
setup.caption: 2. Count the teeth on the pedal gear, starting at the tape.

setup.art: A grown-up turning the pedal slowly one full turn while a child watches the tape on the back tyre go round.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the pedal one full turn. Count the turns of the tape on the tyre.

setup.art: A results table with the counted turns beside the worked-out turns, both close to the same number.
setup.caption: 4. Divide the teeth and compare with what you counted.

flow.do: Show your child the bicycle. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: When I turn the pedals once, how many times will the back wheel turn? Less than once, once, or more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pedal once. How many turns does the wheel make? Why?

ask.q: Do you think the back wheel turns faster or slower than the pedals?
good: Faster, because the bicycle goes fast.
Faster, because the pedal gear is big.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write what they say and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bicycle Gears. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Turn the bicycle over. Stick tape on the back tyre. Stick tape on one tooth of the pedal gear. Count the teeth on the pedal gear and on the small gear at the back wheel.
flow.say: Stick the tape on one tooth, so we know where to start. Count all the teeth on the big gear at the pedals. Then count the teeth on the small gear at the back wheel.
flow.kid: Tape one tooth. Count the teeth on the big gear. Count the teeth on the small gear.
flow.parent: Many single-speed cycles have about 40 to 48 teeth at the pedals and 16 to 20 at the back. If your cycle has many gears, use the gear that the chain is on. Counting the back teeth is easiest if you mark one with tape as well.

check.q: Why do you stick tape on one tooth before counting?
options: So you know where you started and do not count a tooth twice
So the chain does not slip
check.why: The teeth go round in a circle, so there is no end. A mark shows where you began, so you stop at the right place.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the bicycle and count the teeth.

flow.do: Turn the pedal slowly through one full turn, until the taped tooth is back where it began. Your child counts how many times the taped tyre goes round. Do it three times.
flow.say: I will turn the pedal once, slowly. You watch the tape on the tyre. How many times does it go round? Now we do it twice more. Do you get the same number each time?
flow.kid: Watch the tape on the tyre. How many times does it go round for one pedal turn?

ask.q: Why do we do it three times?
good: To check we get the same number.
One try could be a mistake.
So we can trust the answer.

flow.parent: A turn of 2 and a bit is normal. Count part-turns as halves or quarters. The wheel keeps turning after you stop pedalling, so stop the pedal exactly at the mark.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the pedal once and count the turns of the wheel.

flow.do: Divide the teeth on the pedal gear by the teeth on the back gear. Write the answer next to your counted turns. If you have a gear change, move to another gear and try again.
flow.say: Divide the big number by the small number. Is the answer close to what you counted? If it is not, what could have gone wrong?
flow.kid: Big gear teeth divided by small gear teeth. Is it near what you counted?

check.q: A bicycle has 44 teeth at the pedals and 20 at the back. About how many turns does the back wheel make for one pedal turn?
check.why: 44 divided by 20 is 2.2. Picking 1 turn means the gears were thought to be the same size. Picking 20 turns means the numbers were not divided.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the gear ratio from the teeth.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. If your cycle has gears, ask which gear they would use for a hill.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you count? Why do you think the wheel turned that many times?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Would you choose a bigger or a smaller gear at the back for a hill? Why?
flow.parent: A strong answer says the wheel turns more than once, because the pedal gear has more teeth than the back gear. After they have said what they saw, add this: a bigger gear at the back gives fewer turns of the wheel for each pedal turn, but each turn is stronger. That is why people choose it for hills.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bicycle Gears. You explain what you found.

activities.title: Paper Screw: wind a ramp round a pencil

materials.item: 2 sheets of plain paper, and scissors
a ruler and a pencil
a jam jar with its lid, or any bottle with a screw cap
coloured pens
tape

schedule.what: Cut two ramps. Wind them round a pencil. Count the turns and measure the gap. Compare with a real screw.

activities.record: A table with two paper screws, how many turns each made and the gap between the threads. Then a note on the real screw thread you measured.
activities.context: In this activity, you cut two paper ramps with the same length and different heights, wind them round a pencil and see what each makes.

setup.art: Two paper right-angled triangles with the same long side of 20 centimetres, one 2 centimetres tall and one 4 centimetres tall, with the slopes coloured.
setup.caption: 1. Cut two triangles with the same base. One is tall, one is short.

setup.art: A paper triangle being rolled round a pencil, with the coloured slope winding into a spiral.
setup.caption: 2. Roll each triangle round a pencil, starting with its short side.

setup.art: A ruler beside the pencil measuring the gap between two turns of the coloured spiral.
setup.caption: 3. Count the turns and measure the gap.

flow.do: Cut two right-angled triangles from paper. Both are 20 centimetres long on the bottom edge. One is 2 centimetres tall at the end, and the other is 4 centimetres tall. Colour the sloping edge of each.
flow.say: These two ramps are the same length, but one is steeper. We will wind each round a pencil. Which one do you think will make the spiral with the bigger gaps? Why?
flow.kid: Cut two paper ramps. One is steep. One is gentle. Colour the slopes. Guess which has bigger gaps.

ask.q: Which paper ramp will have the bigger gaps between its turns?
good: The steeper one, because it climbs more.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Screw. You cut the ramps and guess.

flow.do: Lay the short edge of the gentle ramp along a pencil. Roll the paper tightly round the pencil, keeping the bottom edge level. Tape the end. Do the same with the steep ramp on a second pencil, or on the same pencil afterwards.
flow.say: Keep the short edge along the pencil. Roll the paper round tightly. The coloured edge makes a spiral. What does it look like?
flow.kid: Roll each ramp round a pencil. The coloured edge makes a spiral.
flow.parent: Keep the bottom edge straight as you roll. If the paper wanders, the spiral will be uneven.
flow.context: In this step, you wind each paper ramp round a pencil.

flow.do: Count the turns of the coloured spiral on each pencil. Measure the gap between two turns in millimetres. Write both in a table.
flow.say: Count the turns of the colour. Then measure the gap from one turn to the next. Which screw has the bigger gap? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Count the turns. Measure the gap. Which is bigger?

check.q: Both ramps are 20 centimetres long. The steeper ramp winds into a spiral with bigger gaps between the turns. What does this show?
options: A steeper ramp makes a screw that moves further in each turn
A steeper ramp makes a stronger screw
check.why: A steeper ramp climbs more in every turn, so the gap, or pitch, is bigger. A gentler ramp has a smaller pitch, and needs more turns to go the same distance, but each turn takes less push.

flow.context: In this step, you count the turns and measure the gap.

flow.do: Look at the thread inside a jam jar lid or on the neck of a bottle. Count how many full turns the lid needs to come off. Measure how far the lid rises, and divide by the turns.
flow.say: Now look at a real screw. Count the full turns to take the lid off. How far does it rise? Divide that by the turns. That is the pitch. Is it big or small?
flow.kid: Count the turns to open the lid. Is the gap big or small?
flow.think: Would a screw with a smaller pitch need more turns or fewer? Would it be easier or harder to turn?
flow.parent: A jam jar lid often rises 2 to 4 millimetres per turn. A bottle cap often needs about one full turn.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Paper Screw. You compare your paper screw with a real one.

activities.title: Clock Gears: why does the hour hand go 12 times slower?

materials.item: an analogue clock or alarm clock with a knob for setting the time, and a grown-up to say it can be turned
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Turn the minute hand round, count the turns, and watch the hour hand.

activities.record: How many times the minute hand went round while the hour hand went round once, and what that tells you about the gears inside.
activities.context: In this activity, you turn the hands of a clock and find the gear ratio hidden inside it.

setup.art: An alarm clock with the hour hand and the minute hand both pointing at 12.
setup.caption: 1. Start with both hands at 12.

setup.art: A finger turning the setting knob at the back of the clock while the minute hand goes round.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the knob slowly and count the turns of the minute hand.

setup.art: The hour hand at 1 o'clock after the minute hand has gone round once.
setup.caption: 3. Watch how far the hour hand has moved.

flow.do: Set both hands of the clock to 12. Ask your child for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Both hands start at 12. The minute hand will go round and round. How many times must it go round before the hour hand goes round once? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Both hands at 12. How many minute turns for one hour-hand turn? Why?

ask.q: How many times do you think the minute hand goes round for one turn of the hour hand?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clock Gears. You guess before you turn.

flow.do: Turn the setting knob slowly, with a grown-up. Watch the hour hand. Count the turns of the minute hand until the hour hand reaches 12 again. Write the number down.
flow.say: Turn the knob slowly. Each time the long hand reaches 12, make a mark. How many marks before the short hand is back at 12?
flow.kid: Turn the knob slowly. Count each time the long hand reaches 12.
flow.parent: Only turn the knob in the direction that the clock allows, and never force it. If your clock cannot be turned, watch a real clock for one hour, and see how far the hour hand moves.

check.q: The minute hand goes round 12 times while the hour hand goes round once. What is the gear ratio between them?
check.why: The minute hand turns 12 times for one turn of the hour hand, so the ratio is 12 to 1. A ratio of 60 to 1 is between the second hand and the minute hand.

flow.context: In this step, you turn the hands and count.

flow.do: Ask your child what they saw and why. Tell them that the second hand goes round 60 times for one turn of the minute hand. Ask what ratio that is.
flow.say: Tell me what you saw. The hour hand turns 12 times slower than the minute hand. What do you think is inside the clock to do that?
flow.kid: The hour hand is 12 times slower. What is inside to do that?
flow.think: A gear train multiplies the ratios. If one pair of gears gives 3 to 1 and another gives 4 to 1, what ratio do they give together?
flow.parent: The answer is 12 to 1, because 3 times 4 is 12. Many clocks reach 12 to 1 with two pairs of gears. This is how compound machines multiply.
flow.context: This is the last step of Clock Gears. You think about what is inside.

activities.title: Kitchen Machine Detective: what is inside a scissors, a peeler and a pressure cooker?

materials.item: a scissors, a vegetable peeler, a bottle opener or can opener, a pressure cooker lid, a tap or door handle
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Take each tool, find its simple machines and say what it trades.

activities.record: A table with the tool, the simple machines inside it, and what each one trades.
activities.context: In this activity, you take everyday tools and find the simple machines hidden inside them.

setup.art: A table with a scissors, a peeler, a bottle opener, a pressure cooker lid and a tap laid out in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out five tools from the kitchen and the house.

setup.art: A child looking closely at a scissors with an arrow on the fulcrum and another on the blade edge.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely and find the simple machines inside each.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a table of tools, machines and trades.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the table.

flow.do: Lay out the five tools. Ask your child to pick one and to say what it does. Ask which simple machines might be inside.
flow.say: Pick any one of these tools. What does it do? Which of the six machines, lever, pulley, wheel and axle, ramp, wedge or screw, might be hiding inside it?
flow.kid: Pick a tool. What does it do? Which machines are hiding inside?

ask.q: Which simple machines can you spot in a pair of scissors?
good: The screw in the middle holds them.

flow.parent: Scissors have two levers joined at a screw or rivet, and each blade is a wedge. A peeler has a wedge blade and a lever handle. A can opener has a wheel and axle with a handle, a wedge and a lever. A pressure cooker lid locks with a screw-like twist. A tap has a screw inside it and a wheel and axle for the handle.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Machine Detective. You pick a tool and guess.

flow.do: Look closely at each tool, one at a time. Write down every simple machine you can find and what it trades, force for distance or turns for strength. A grown-up should handle the blades.
flow.say: For each tool, find each machine. For each machine, say what it trades. Does it make your push stronger, or does it make your hand move further?
flow.kid: Find each machine in each tool. Say what it trades.

check.q: A scissors cuts thick card more easily near the screw than near the tips. Why?
options: The load is closer to the fulcrum, so the same push gives a bigger cut
check.why: A scissors is a lever. The screw is the fulcrum. A load close to the fulcrum gets a bigger force from the same push at the handles, just as a coin close to the pencil on a ruler. Picking 'tips are blunter' means the lever was not noticed.

flow.context: In this step, you look for machines inside each tool.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose the tool with the most machines. Ask where the friction is, and what a drop of oil would do.
flow.say: Which tool has the most machines inside? Where do you think the rubbing is? What would a drop of oil do?
flow.kid: Which tool has most machines? Where is the rubbing?
flow.think: If a tool has three machines, each 90 percent efficient, how much of your effort comes out?
flow.parent: The answer is about 73 percent, because 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 is 0.729. Each part loses a share.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Kitchen Machine Detective. You think about friction.

activities.title: Rope Count at Home and Outside: where are the hidden pulleys?

materials.item: paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Go round the home and look outside. Find pulleys, count the ropes, and say what each does.

activities.record: A list of at least five places with a pulley, how many ropes hold the load, and whether the pulley turns the pull or shrinks it.
activities.context: In this activity, you hunt for pulleys in your home and street and count the ropes.

setup.art: A ceiling clothes drying rack with a rope and two small pulleys, raised high above a room.
setup.caption: 1. Look for a clothes rack, a curtain cord or a window blind.

setup.art: A tower crane at a building site with its hook and rope, seen from the street.
setup.caption: 2. Look outside for a crane, a lift or a well.

setup.art: A paper list with the place, the ropes counted and whether it turns or shrinks the pull.
setup.caption: 3. Write down what you find.

flow.do: Walk round your home. Look for a ceiling clothes rack, a curtain cord, a window blind, a flagpole or a well. Write down each place.
flow.say: Look for a rope that goes over a wheel. Where is one in our home? Let us walk round and look.
flow.kid: Look for a rope over a wheel. Where is one in our home?

ask.q: Where would you expect to find a pulley in a home?

flow.parent: A ceiling clothes drying rack has a rope and two or more small pulleys. Pull the rope down and the rack rises. Count the ropes that hold the rack.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rope Count. You look inside the home.

flow.do: Pick two of the pulleys you found. Count the ropes that hold each load. Say whether the pulley turns the pull or makes it smaller. Look outside from a window or the street at a crane, a lift or a well.
flow.say: Count the ropes that hold the load. If the rope only turns round the top, it does not count. Does it make the pull smaller, or only turn it?
flow.kid: Count the ropes holding the load. Does it turn the pull or make it smaller?

check.q: A clothes rack hangs from 4 ropes, and a rope goes over small wheels to your hand. About how much of the load do you pull?
options: About a quarter of the load
check.why: Four ropes hold the rack, so each carries about a quarter and you pull about a quarter, with some more for friction. The price is that you pull about four times as much rope as the rack rises.

flow.parent: Stay on the pavement or at a window when you look at building sites. A tower crane often has several ropes on its hook block, so it has a big advantage. Never go near the site itself.
flow.context: In this step, you count the ropes.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose the neatest pulley they found, and to say why it was a good idea.
flow.say: Which pulley is the neatest? What problem does it solve? What would it be like without it?
flow.kid: Which pulley is neatest? What problem does it solve?
flow.think: Why do tall cranes use many ropes on their hook, while a flagpole uses just one?
flow.parent: A flag is light, so the direction is all that matters. A crane lifts a heavy load, so the advantage matters.
flow.context: This is the last step of Rope Count. You think about why each pulley was chosen.

projects.title: Charkha Belt Drive: a big wheel that turns a small wheel fast

materials.item: a shoebox or a stiff cardboard box
2 pencils or thin sticks for axles
stiff card for a big wheel, 12 centimetres across, and a small wheel, 3 centimetres across
a loop of strong thread or a thin rubber band, for the belt
scissors, a ruler, tape and a coloured pen
2 drinking straws, to hold the axles

schedule.what: Build the wheels and the box frame. Fit the belt. Turn the big wheel and count the turns of the small one.

projects.record: Draw the belt drive, with the sizes of the wheels, and write how many times the small wheel turned for each turn of the big wheel.
projects.context: In this project, you build a simple belt drive like the one on a charkha and find how many times the small wheel turns for one turn of the big wheel.

setup.art: Two card wheels, a big one and a small one, each with a hole in the centre and a pencil through it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a big wheel and a small wheel. Push a pencil through each centre.

setup.art: A shoebox with two straws taped across it and the two pencils through the straws, holding the wheels.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the straws to the box. Slide each pencil through a straw.

setup.art: A loop of thread running round both wheels, with the big wheel being turned by a hand.
setup.caption: 3. Loop the belt round both wheels and turn the big wheel.

flow.do: Show your child a picture or the memory of a charkha. Ask for a guess and a reason. The big wheel is 12 centimetres across and the small one is 3 centimetres across.
flow.say: On a charkha, a big wheel turns a thin spindle. If I turn the big wheel once, how many times will the small wheel turn? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Big wheel turns once. How many turns for the small wheel? Why?

ask.q: Will the small wheel turn more or fewer times than the big one?
good: More, because the belt has to go round it too.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The answer is 4, because the big wheel is 4 times as wide.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Charkha Belt Drive. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Cut the two wheels from stiff card. Poke a hole in the centre of each. Push a pencil through each hole and tape it so it spins with the wheel. Colour a mark on the edge of each wheel.
flow.say: Cut a big circle and a small circle. Push a pencil through the middle of each. Colour a mark on the edge, so we can count the turns.
flow.kid: Cut two circles. Push a pencil through each. Mark each edge.
flow.parent: The hole must be exactly in the centre, or the wheel wobbles. Fold a circle in half twice to find its centre.
flow.context: In this step, you build the two wheels.

flow.do: Tape a straw across the box near each end. Slide each pencil through a straw so the wheels sit side by side. Put the belt round both wheels. Slide the pencils apart until the belt is tight.
flow.say: The straws are the bearings. Put the belt round both wheels and slide them apart until it is tight. Turn the big wheel. Does the small wheel turn?
flow.kid: Pencils through the straws. Belt round both wheels. Pull it tight. Turn the big wheel.
flow.parent: If the belt slips, wrap a rubber band round the rim of each wheel for grip. If the wheels rub on the box, tape a bit of card between them.
flow.context: In this step, you fit the belt.

flow.do: Turn the big wheel exactly 5 times, slowly. Your child counts how many times the small wheel's mark goes round. Divide it by 5. Compare with the guess.
flow.say: Turn the big wheel five times, slowly. Count how many times the small wheel's mark goes round. How many turns for each big turn?
flow.kid: Turn the big wheel 5 times. Count the small wheel's turns.

check.q: A big wheel 12 centimetres across drives a small wheel 3 centimetres across with a belt. How many times does the small wheel turn for one big turn?
check.why: 12 divided by 3 is 4. Each time the big wheel turns once, it pulls the belt by its whole rim, and that is enough to turn the small rim 4 times. Picking 12 means the sizes were not divided.

flow.context: In this step, you count the turns and find the ratio.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Ask what would happen if they swapped the wheels.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why? What if the small wheel drove the big one?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. What if you swapped them?
flow.think: If the small wheel drives the big one, does the big wheel turn faster or slower? Is it easier or harder to turn?
flow.parent: The big wheel would turn 4 times slower, but with more strength. A charkha turns a big wheel slowly with the hand, so the spindle spins very fast.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Charkha Belt Drive. You explain what you found.

challenges.title: The Lazy Lift: raise the bottle with the lightest pull
challenges.problem: Raise a full 1 litre bottle by 10 centimetres so that the rubber band stretches as little as you can make it. You may use up to 3 reels, one length of string and the beam. The bottle must rise at least 10 centimetres and hang still for 5 seconds.
constraints: Use only string, the beam and the rubber band.
The bottle must rise at least 10 centimetres and hang still for 5 seconds.
Write down the band stretch and how far the knot moved.
materials: a broom handle across two chair backs
general: One fixed reel and one moving reel, with two strings holding the bottle, as in Test C.
The same, but with the pull going up, so no fixed reel is needed.
The same set-up with a drop of oil on each reel's string loop, to cut the rubbing.
creative: Hang a second moving reel from the first one's string, so the pull is a quarter, with 3 reels in all.
Use bigger, smoother reels, so there is less rubbing and the band stretches less than the ideal numbers suggest.
Use a different string, such as thread, and test whether friction goes down.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it. Count the strings that hold the bottle. Work out the pull you should get, and measure the real stretch. How close were they? Where did the extra go?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about pulleys. You find the way of raising the bottle that stretches the band least.

setup.art: A child sketching three pulley designs on paper with arrows for the strings.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs. Count the strings holding the bottle.

setup.art: A bottle hanging from two reels, one inside the other's loop, with a rubber band at the loose end held by a hand.
setup.caption: 2. Build your design and lift the bottle 10 centimetres.

setup.art: A table with the stretch of the band and the distance of the knot for each design.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your designs.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three different designs. Ask them to count the strings holding the bottle in each.
flow.say: You have up to three reels. How could you set them up so that the band stretches the least? Draw some ideas first, and count the strings that hold the bottle.
flow.kid: You have 3 reels. Draw some ideas. Count the strings holding the bottle.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Lazy Lift. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Lift the bottle 10 centimetres and hold it for 5 seconds. Read the band's stretch. Measure how far the knot moved. Then change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Build your first design and test it. Read the stretch. Then change one thing, such as the number of strings, and test again. Which change helped?
flow.kid: Build your design. Lift 10 centimetres. Read the stretch. Change one thing.
flow.parent: A cascade of two moving reels, with the second reel hanging from the string of the first, can give a quarter of the pull. The knot then moves about 40 centimetres. Friction is bigger, so expect a stretch somewhat above a quarter. Keep fingers away from the string when the bottle is hanging.

check.q: A design has 4 strings holding the bottle. The band stretches 10 centimetres in the straight lift. About how far should it stretch now, with no friction?
check.why: 10 divided by 4 is 2.5. In real life it is a little more because of rubbing. Picking 40 centimetres means the distance was mixed up with the pull.

flow.context: In this step, you build, test and improve.

flow.do: Compare all your designs. Pick the best and draw it. Work out the force times the distance for the best design, and for the straight lift.
flow.say: Which design gave the smallest stretch? How far did the knot move? Multiply the stretch by the distance for the best design and for the straight lift. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Which design was best? Multiply stretch by distance. Compare with the straight lift.
flow.think: Did the best design cost something? What did you give up to get the smaller pull?
flow.parent: The pull-times-distance numbers should be about the same, or a little bigger for the best design. That is the trade, plus friction.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Lazy Lift. You compare the designs.

items.p: What does a single fixed pulley, such as the wheel over a well, do for you?
opts: It changes the direction of your pull but not its size
items.why: A fixed pulley only turns the pull round, so you pull down to lift up. The pull is the same as the weight of the load. Picking 'lighter' means the pulley was thought to change the load, but the load weighs the same.

items.p: A load hangs from 4 ropes that share it equally. Each rope carries ____ of the load.
items.why: Four equal shares of the load make a quarter each. That is why the pull is a quarter of the load, when there is no friction.

items.p: A load of 24 kilograms is held by 3 ropes. Ignoring friction, how many kilograms does the pull feel like?
items.why: 24 divided by 3 is 8. Each rope carries 8 kilograms, so the pull feels like lifting 8 kilograms.

items.p: A moving pulley makes the load itself weigh less.
items.why: False. The load weighs the same. A moving pulley makes two ropes share the load, so each rope, and your hand, carries only a share.

items.p: A bottle hangs from a moving pulley with 2 ropes holding it. To lift the bottle by 10 centimetres, how far must the free end of the rope move?
items.why: Both ropes must get 10 centimetres shorter, so 20 centimetres of rope must pass through your hand. A smaller pull always goes a longer way.

items.p: When a machine makes a force smaller, which thing does it keep the same on both sides?
opts: The force multiplied by the distance
items.why: Force times distance, which scientists call work, is the same on both sides. If the force halves, the distance doubles.

items.p: Force multiplied by distance is called ____.
items.why: In science, work is the force on a thing times the distance it moves in the direction of the force.

items.p: Sort each machine by what it does to your pull or push.
items: a flagpole pulley with one rope
a single wheel over a well
a block and tackle with 4 ropes
a crowbar with a long handle
a clothes rack lifted by 4 ropes
items.why: A single fixed wheel only changes the direction. A tackle with several ropes, a long ramp and a long lever each make the force smaller, and each pays for it in distance.

items.p: Match each everyday thing to the simple machine inside it.
items.why: A scissors is two levers joined at a pivot, each with a wedge blade. A lid has a thread, which is a ramp wound round. A knife is a wedge. A clothes rack uses pulleys. A bicycle chain wheel has teeth, so it is a gear.

items.p: In real tests, the pull is always a little more than the ideal numbers say. What is the best reason?
opts: Friction turns some of your effort into warmth
items.why: Rubbing at the axles and ropes turns part of the work into warmth that spreads into the air. Picking 'load gets heavier' means the load was thought to change, but the load stays the same.

items.p: Putting oil on the axle of a pulley reduces the pull you need.
items.why: True. Oil reduces the rubbing, so less of your work turns into warmth.

items.p: A bicycle has 40 teeth on the pedal gear and 20 teeth on the back gear. How many times does the back wheel turn for one turn of the pedals?
items.why: 40 divided by 20 is 2. For each turn of the pedals, the chain moves 40 teeth, which turns the 20-tooth gear twice.

items.p: A small gear drives a big gear. What happens to the big gear?
opts: It turns more slowly, but with more strength
It turns faster, with more strength
It turns at the same speed
items.why: The big gear turns fewer times for each turn of the small gear. What it loses in speed it gains in turning strength.

items.p: A friend says, 'With two ropes, you do half the work.' Say what is right and what is wrong in what she says.
items.a: She is right that the pull is half. She is wrong about the work. The hand moves twice as far, so force times distance is the same.
items.why: A strong answer says the pull halves, the distance doubles and the work stays the same, apart from friction.

items.p: Draw a bottle hanging from a moving pulley with 2 ropes. Draw an arrow on each rope. If the bottle weighs 10 newtons, write the pull in each rope.
items.a: A bottle hanging from a wheel in a loop of rope, with two upward arrows on the two ropes, each labelled 5 newtons.
items.why: Two ropes share the 10 newtons equally, so each carries 5 newtons. A strong drawing shows two ropes holding the wheel and both arrows the same length.

items.p: A jam jar lid goes down 3 millimetres each turn. Say in your own words why a lid is a ramp.
items.a: The thread inside the lid is a ramp wound round and round. Each turn climbs one small slope, so the lid moves slowly and firmly.
items.why: A strong answer says the thread is a ramp wound round, and each turn climbs a little, so a small twist gives a strong push.

items.p: These are made-up results from the bottle lift. How many centimetres less did the band stretch in Test C than in Test A?

chart.title: Band stretch for each way of lifting the bottle

items.why: The bar for A is 8 and the bar for C is 5. 8 take away 5 is 3 centimetres less.

items.p: In the same results, Test C stretched the band 5 centimetres, but exactly half of A would be 4. What is the best reason for the difference?
opts: Friction used up a little of the work
items.why: Rubbing at the reel and the string turned a little of the work into warmth, so the pull had to be a little larger. The ideal numbers are the best case with no rubbing.

items.p: An ideal tackle has 5 ropes and a load of 60 kilograms. In real life you pull with 15 kilograms. The ideal pull is 12. What percent of your effort is useful?
items.why: Useful share is 12 divided by 15, which is 0.8, or 80 percent. The other 20 percent turned into warmth.

items.p: A bucket is lifted 3 metres with a tackle that has 3 ropes holding it. How many metres of rope must pass through your hands?
items.why: 3 ropes each get 3 metres shorter, so 3 times 3 is 9 metres of rope.

items.p: A load is lifted by 4 ropes. To raise it 1 metre, how much rope must you pull?
items.why: Each of the 4 ropes gets 1 metre shorter, so 4 metres of rope must come through your hand. The pull is a quarter, and the distance is 4 times.

items.p: Put these in the right order for how a ceiling clothes rack goes up when you pull the rope.
a: The rope runs over the small wheels
The ropes holding the rack get shorter
items.why: Your pull goes down the rope, over the wheels, shortens the ropes that hold the rack, and the rack goes up. The rope you pull is longer than the distance the rack rises.

items.p: A gear with 48 teeth drives a gear with 12 teeth. The big gear turns 3 times. How many times does the small gear turn?
items.why: 48 divided by 12 is 4 turns for each turn of the big gear. 3 turns of the big gear give 3 times 4, which is 12. Picking 4 forgets the 3 turns.

items.p: A screw moves forward 3 millimetres in each turn. This distance is called the ____ of the screw.
items.why: The pitch is the distance a screw moves forward in one full turn. It is the gap between one thread and the next.

items.p: A thin wedge multiplies your push more than a thick wedge does.
items.why: True. A thin wedge has longer, gentler sloping sides, so it multiplies the push more, like a gentle ramp.

items.p: Match each machine to what it really is.
pairs: a ramp wound round a rod
a lever with arms in a ratio of 2 to 1
items.why: A handle turns a wheel as a long lever arm turns the axle. A screw's thread is a ramp wound round. A wedge is two ramps. A moving pulley has the load in the middle and your pull at the end, so the arms are 1 and 2.

items.p: Sort each machine into the lever family or the ramp family.
items.why: The see-saw, the wheel and axle and the pulley all work like a lever. The screw, the wedge and the slope all work like a ramp.

items.p: Why can a machine never give out more work than it takes in?
opts: Energy is never made from nothing, so a machine can only pass it on
items.why: Work is a way of counting energy being passed on. Energy cannot be made from nothing, so the work out cannot be more than the work in.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a bottle lift. Label the three parts: the fixed wheel, the moving wheel and the load.
labels: Wheel that rises with the bottle
items.art: A beam with one wheel hanging from it, a bottle hanging from a second wheel in a loop of string, and a string running over the first wheel to a hand.
a: Wheel hung from the beam: fixed wheel
Wheel that rises with the bottle: moving wheel
items.why: The wheel hung from the beam stays still, so it is fixed. The wheel the bottle hangs from rises with it, so it is moving. The bottle is the load.

items.p: Karthika and Zaid are building a pulley system to lift a heavy bag.

views.who: Karthika, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Add as many pulleys as we can. Every pulley makes the job easier.

views.who: Zaid, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Each pulley adds rubbing. After a few, the extra rubbing eats up what we gain.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? How could you test it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a fair test, such as adding one pulley at a time and measuring the pull each time.
items.why: Both have a point. More ropes give a smaller ideal pull, but each pulley adds friction, so the real gain gets smaller. A fair test adds one pulley at a time and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: Explain, using the words ropes, pull and distance, why a crane has a block and tackle with many ropes.
items.a: The load is shared between many ropes, so each rope carries a small part and the pull is small. The price is that a long length of rope must be pulled for a short lift.
items.why: A strong answer says more ropes share the load, so the pull is smaller, and that the rope pulled is much longer than the lift.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Wedge, screw, slope, lever.
items.a: Lever, because the other three belong to the ramp family.
items.why: A wedge, a screw and a slope all work like a ramp. A lever works by turning round a fulcrum.

items.p: A cyclist reaches a steep hill. Should she change to a bigger or a smaller gear at the back? Explain.
items.a: A bigger gear at the back. The wheel turns fewer times for each pedal turn, but with more strength, which helps up the hill.
items.why: A strong answer says the big back gear gives more turning strength and fewer wheel turns for each pedal turn, which is the same trade of speed for strength.

items.p: You pull with the strength of 6 kilograms on a tackle with 5 ropes holding the load. Ignoring friction, how many kilograms is the load?
items.why: 5 ropes each carry 6 kilograms, so the load is 5 times 6, which is 30 kilograms.

items.p: Two machines are joined, so that one drives the other. Each wastes one tenth of the work. What percent of your work comes out at the end?
items.why: The first leaves 0.9. The second leaves 0.9 of that. 0.9 times 0.9 is 0.81, which is 81 percent.

items.p: A bicycle has 48 teeth at the pedals. The back wheel has gears of 24, 16 and 12 teeth. For the 12-tooth gear, how many wheel turns do you get for one pedal turn?
items.why: 48 divided by 12 is 4. The smallest back gear gives the most wheel turns for each pedal turn.

items.p: A screw has a pitch of 1.5 millimetres. How many full turns move it 12 millimetres?
items.why: 12 divided by 1.5 is 8. Each turn moves it 1.5 millimetres, so 8 turns move it 12.

items.p: A lever has a push arm 100 times as long as its load arm. Your end moves 50 centimetres. How far does the load move, in centimetres?
items.why: The load moves 100 times less than your end. 50 divided by 100 is 0.5 centimetres.

items.p: On the same lever, you push down with the strength of 1 kilogram. What is the biggest load, ignoring friction, that you can balance?
items.why: The push arm is 100 times longer, so the load can be 100 times bigger. The price is that your end moves 100 times further.

items.p: Two pairs of gears are joined in a train. One pair gives 3 turns for each turn, and the next pair gives 4. How many turns does the last gear make for one turn of the first?
items.why: The ratios multiply, so 3 times 4 is 12. Many clocks use this to make the minute hand turn 12 times for each turn of the hour hand.

items.p: Nobody has ever built a machine that is 100 percent efficient.
items.why: True. There is always some friction, so some work always turns into warmth.

items.p: Emmy Noether showed in 1918 that energy cannot be made from nothing if which thing is true?
opts: The laws of nature are the same on every day
items.why: Her theorem links the saving of energy to the laws of nature not changing with time. It is a deep reason behind the rule that no machine gives out more than it takes in.

items.p: In 1974, scientists stuck a bacterium's thread to a glass slide and the whole cell spun round. What did this show?
opts: The thread is turned by a tiny rotary motor at its base
The cell was alive and stuck
The thread is a tiny lever
items.why: If the thread is fixed, a motor at its base can only spin the whole cell round. It showed that the thread turns like a propeller, not by waving.

items.p: The scientists' unit for work and energy is the ____.
items.why: One joule is the work of pushing with 1 newton through 1 metre.

items.p: A girl lifts a bag with a force of 20 newtons, up by 0.5 metres. How many joules of work does she do?
items.why: Work is force times distance. 20 times 0.5 is 10 joules.

items.p: Archimedes is said to have claimed he could move the Earth with a long enough lever. Say what would be wrong with that plan, using the word distance.
items.a: He would have to push his end an unimaginably long distance for the Earth to move even a tiny bit. The lever would be as long as a galaxy.
items.why: A strong answer says a lever trades force for distance, so a small push on an enormous load needs a huge distance.

items.p: Farida and Ishaan are arguing about a ramp.

views.who: Farida, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A machine needs moving parts. A ramp just sits there, so it is not a machine.

views.who: Ishaan, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A machine is anything that trades a small force for a longer distance. A ramp does that exactly, so it is a machine.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and says what evidence or definition would change their mind.
items.why: It depends on what we mean by a machine. If we mean 'moving parts', a ramp is not one. If we mean 'something that trades force for distance', it is. The disagreement is about the word, not about the ramp.

items.p: Physicists once saw energy go missing in some atoms. Wolfgang Pauli guessed an invisible particle instead of giving up the rule, and it was found 26 years later. Was that cheating or good science? Give one reason.
items.a: It was good science, because the guess could be tested and was found. The rule was kept because it had worked everywhere else, and the new particle was real.
items.why: A strong answer says the guess made a prediction that could be checked, and that it was checked. A weaker answer says it is cheating without noticing that the particle was found.

items.p: Draw a block and tackle with 3 ropes holding a load of 30 newtons. Write the pull in each rope and how far your hand moves for a 1 metre lift.
items.a: A load hanging from a moving block with 3 ropes going up to a fixed block, each rope labelled 10 newtons, and a note that the hand moves 3 metres.
items.why: Three ropes share 30 newtons, so each carries 10 newtons, and the pull is 10 newtons. The hand moves 3 times the lift, which is 3 metres.

items.p: Match each tiny machine to its job.
pairs: The motor at the base of a bacterium's thread
spins the thread so the bacterium swims
turns to make the cell's fuel molecule ATP
The head of a muscle protein
pulls like a tiny lever to shorten the muscle
items.why: A bacterium swims by spinning a thread with a rotary motor. ATP synthase turns like a wheel on an axle to make ATP. A muscle protein pulls like a tiny lever to shorten the muscle.

quiz.p: A flagpole has one pulley at the top. What does it do for you?
opts: It lets you pull down to raise the flag
It makes the flag weigh less
quiz.why: A single fixed pulley changes the direction of the pull, so you pull down and the flag goes up. It does not change the size of the pull.

quiz.p: A load is held by 4 ropes. You pull with the strength of 5 kilograms. What is the load, ignoring friction?
quiz.why: 4 ropes each carry 5 kilograms, so the load is 4 times 5, which is 20 kilograms. Picking 9 means the numbers were added.

quiz.p: To lift a load by 2 metres with a tackle with 2 ropes holding it, how much rope must you pull?
quiz.why: Both ropes must get 2 metres shorter, so 4 metres pass through your hand.

quiz.p: A machine halves the force you need. What must happen to the distance you move?
quiz.why: Force times distance stays the same, so if the force halves, the distance doubles. No machine gives a smaller force over the same distance.

quiz.p: Where does some of your effort go in a real pulley?
quiz.why: Friction turns some of the work into warmth that spreads into the air. The energy is not destroyed. It goes somewhere you did not want it.

quiz.p: Two machines are used together, and each wastes one tenth of the work. About how much of the work comes out?
quiz.why: 0.9 times 0.9 is 0.81. Losses multiply, so more machines can be worse.

quiz.p: A cyclist moves the chain from a 16-tooth to a 24-tooth gear at the back. What happens to the wheel?
opts: It turns fewer times for each pedal turn, with more strength
It turns more times for each pedal turn
It turns the same number of times
quiz.why: A bigger back gear means a smaller ratio, so fewer wheel turns for each pedal turn. The wheel gains turning strength, which helps uphill.

opts: A ramp wound round a rod
quiz.why: The thread of a screw is a ramp that goes round and round. That is why a small twist gives a strong push forward.

quiz.p: A blunt knife needs more push than a sharp knife, because a blunt edge is a thicker wedge.
quiz.why: True. A thick wedge has steeper sides, so it multiplies the push less. Sharpening makes the wedge thinner.

quiz.p: The six simple machines are really which two ideas?
quiz.why: The pulley and the wheel and axle are kinds of lever. The wedge and the screw are kinds of ramp. Both trade force for distance.

quiz.p: Why did we do each set-up of the bottle lift twice?
opts: To check that the result is steady and not a fluke
quiz.why: If two tries are close, we can trust the result. If they differ a lot, one try may have been a fluke, and we need to look for the cause.

quiz.p: Why has nobody built a machine that gives out more work than it takes in?
opts: Energy cannot be made from nothing, so a machine only passes it on
quiz.why: Every careful test has shown the same result. Physicists link it to the laws of nature being the same on every day.

open_questions.q: Is energy conserved in the whole expanding universe?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists agree that it is conserved in every small region we can measure, but in an expanding universe the definition becomes hard, and they are still discussing it.

open_questions.q: How did the Antikythera mechanism's makers learn to cut such small gears so well?
open_questions.why_open: No written plans survive, and no other machine as complex is known for over a thousand years.
Rope and wood rot, so very few pulleys survive, and the oldest ones we know are probably not the first.

open_questions.q: How do the tiny motors in cells turn so efficiently?
open_questions.why_open: Some motors turn with almost no waste. Scientists are still working out how, and engineers are trying to copy them.

open_questions.q: Could a machine ever be built with no friction at all?
open_questions.why_open: Some magnetic and very cold systems come close, but nothing is exactly frictionless, and nobody knows how close we can get.

open_questions.q: Why did no large animal evolve wheels?
open_questions.why_open: A wheel needs a clear path round it, so blood and nerves cannot cross. Scientists still discuss other reasons, and whether some living things come close.

maths.problem: In the bottle lift, the band stretched 9 centimetres in the straight lift and 5 centimetres with the moving reel. How many centimetres less was the stretch with the moving reel?
maths.explain: 9 take away 5 is 4. The moving reel made the band stretch 4 centimetres less.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, you hang a bottle from a rubber band and read how far the band stretches.
maths.why_maths: A subtraction shows how much a machine helped, so you can compare set-ups.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart of made-up results. Is the stretch for Test C a little more than half, or a little less than half, of the stretch for Test A?
maths.explain: Test A is 9 and half of 9 is 4 and a half. Test C is 5, which is a little more than 4 and a half. The extra comes from friction.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, Test A is the straight lift, Test B uses one fixed reel and Test C uses a moving reel. The chart shows made-up results.

chart.title: Band stretch for each way of lifting the bottle

maths.why_maths: Comparing a result with half shows whether the machine did what the ideal rule says, and how much friction took.

maths.problem: A tackle has 5 ropes and a load of 40 kilograms. Ignoring friction, what is the pull? In real life you pull with the strength of 10 kilograms. What percent of your effort is useful?
maths.explain: 40 divided by 5 is 8. The useful share is 8 divided by 10, which is 0.8, or 80 percent.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, the real pull was always a little more than the ideal pull, because of friction.
maths.why_maths: A percent turns the gap between the ideal and the real pull into one number that compares machines.

maths.problem: In the bottle lift, the knot moved 20 centimetres for a 10 centimetre lift with 2 ropes. How far would it move for a 30 centimetre lift with 4 ropes holding the load?
maths.explain: With 4 ropes the knot moves 4 times the lift. 4 times 30 is 120 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, the more ropes hold the bottle, the further the knot moves.
maths.why_maths: A multiplication predicts how much rope you must pull, before you build the machine.

maths.problem: A bicycle has 48 teeth on the pedal gear and 16 on the back gear. You turn the pedals 10 times. The wheel goes 2 metres in each turn. How far does the bicycle go?
maths.explain: 48 divided by 16 is 3, so the wheel turns 3 times for each pedal turn. 10 times 3 is 30 wheel turns. 30 times 2 is 60 metres.
maths.context: In the Bicycle Gears test, you find how many times the wheel turns for one turn of the pedals.
maths.why_maths: A gear ratio turns pedal turns into distance travelled, so you can plan a ride.

maths.problem: A girl lifts a 2 kilogram bag, which pulls down with about 20 newtons, up by 0.5 metres. How many joules of work is that? Then she lifts the same bag by the same height with a 4-rope tackle. What pull does she use, and how far does her hand move?
maths.answer: 10 joules. A pull of 5 newtons and 2 metres.
maths.explain: 20 times 0.5 is 10 joules. With 4 ropes, the pull is 20 divided by 4, which is 5 newtons. The hand moves 4 times 0.5, which is 2 metres. 5 times 2 is 10 joules again.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, you saw that force times distance stays the same.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying force by distance shows that the work does not change when you add ropes.

maths.problem: A screw has a pitch of 1.5 millimetres. How many full turns move it 12 millimetres?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 1.5 is 8. Each turn moves it 1.5 millimetres, so 8 turns move it 12 millimetres.
maths.context: In the Paper Screw activity, you measured the gap between two turns of a thread.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the distance by the pitch tells you how many turns a screw needs.

maths.problem: A lever has a push arm 1000 times as long as its load arm. What is the biggest load, in kilograms, that a 50 kilogram person could balance by pushing with all their weight? How far would their end move for the load to move 1 centimetre?
maths.explain: 50 times 1000 is 50,000 kilograms. Their end moves 1000 times as far as the load, so 1 centimetre of lift needs 1000 centimetres of push, which is 10 metres.
maths.context: In the Count the Ropes test, you saw that a smaller force always goes a longer distance. A very long lever makes the idea big.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers show why a lever that could move the Earth would need a push as long as a galaxy.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,300 years ago, a short Greek book called Mechanical Problems asked why a small push can lift a heavy stone with a lever. Its unknown author called this a wonder, a trick played on nature, and explained it by saying that the long end of a lever moves along a bigger circle. Many people after that believed a clever machine could win something for nothing. In the 1590s, an Italian teacher named Galileo Galilei wrote a short work for his students called Le Meccaniche. He went through the lever, the pulley, the wheel and axle, the screw and the ramp. He showed that every one of them follows one rule. What a machine gains in force, it loses in distance. So there is no trick and no wonder, only a trade. The rule was later written in the language of energy.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian teacher and scientist (1564 to 1642), answering a Greek book of about 2,300 years before
how_we_found_out.when: Mechanical Problems, about 300 BCE. Le Meccaniche, in the 1590s.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Greek book called the lever a wonder that beats nature, and many people thought a clever machine could win something for free. Galileo showed that every machine pays for a smaller force with a longer distance.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Count the Ropes: the string-through-the-reel loop pulleys and the rubber band gauge are the most likely thing to need adjusting. The band should stretch 6 to 12 centimetres under the full bottle. If it stretches less than 4 or reaches its limit, the steps say what to change. The stretch with the moving reel should be a little more than half, and the knot should move about 20 centimetres. Because the band is not exactly even, the numbers show the pattern, not exact halves. Bicycle Gears needs a grown-up to turn the bicycle over. Clock Gears needs a clock with a setting knob. The Paper Screw gaps depend on how tightly the paper is wound. Facts to check before the unit goes live: the Ljubljana Marshes wheel (about 5,000 years old, found in 2002), the earliest pulleys (Mesopotamia and Egypt, about 3,500 years ago), that Emmy Noether's early lectures were announced under David Hilbert's name, that the mote (Karnataka) and charsa (North India) are the right names for the bullock-drawn leather bucket lifts, the single-speed bicycle tooth counts in the notes, and the Galileo and Mechanical Problems dates.
